metadata.title: The Tokenization Problem
metadata.purpose: STEM & AI Architecture, Week 6 — why a trillion-parameter model cannot reliably format a number: tokens are not quantities, formatting is probabilistic, and the only fix is deterministic downstream parsing.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Onkar Bhujbal, and this video is about why the smartest artificial intelligence in the world cannot reliably format basic arithmetic. Ask a language model for a financial figure and it might give you integer digits, a comma-separated string, or a dollar sign with a decimal. Understanding why means looking at how these models actually read data.

output lands — the same quantity, spelled differently each run
the last output line names the cause: THE TOKENIZATION PROBLEM

props.command: Why can't a trillion-parameter model write a number the same way twice?
output: Same quantity. Four spellings. One of them breaks your parser.

beats.honesty_note: The four spellings illustrate the variability the script describes. Not a transcript of any specific model's outputs; no model or product is named.

beats.narration_text: A model has no concept of quantity at all. It is predicting the next fragment of text, and text has many correct-looking spellings for the same amount. So formatting is not something you request. It is something you enforce, afterwards, in code.

beats.narration_text: Large language models do not do math. They do not perceive five million as a quantitative value — they see a sequence of fragmented tokens. Depending on context, the model statistically predicts which fragment should come next. And because human training data contains thousands of ways to write currency, the output is fundamentally probabilistic.

beats.narration_text: This becomes catastrophic in software engineering. Pipe probabilistic output straight into a backend that strictly requires an integer, and a single unexpected dollar sign triggers a fatal type error and takes your application down. You cannot prompt-engineer your way out of this.

beats.narration_text: So let's put a deterministic layer between the model and the database, and watch the same hostile string come out the other side as a number we can actually use.

props.command: Write a parser that turns "$5.0M" into 5000000.0 — and returns None rather than raising when the text is not a number at all.

beats.authoring_note: ASK → RESULT pair: B04 is the ask, B05 is the result (ASK→RESULT LAW).

beats.narration_text: The only secure way to handle model-generated data is downstream deterministic parsing. You insert a regular-expression layer between the model and your database, strip the noise, and extract the core value. But note what the suffix needs. Stripping the M would leave you with five point zero. You have to map it to a multiplier — and that is the difference between five million and five. If the extraction fails, you return nothing, and you drop the payload.
beats.new_visual_element: The hostile string, the parser, and the number that survives

show.event: left panel lands: the raw model output, dollar sign and suffix intact
on 'strip the noise', the non-numeric span highlights terracotta IN PLACE
note lands beneath: the suffix is not noise — it is the magnitude
right panel reveals the parser line by line, the SUFFIX map first
ink stamp lands: 5000000.0 — parsed, not stripped

props.sparkLine: Strip the noise. Keep the magnitude.
props.hotNote: the $ is noise — the M is not
props.stampSub: mapped the suffix to a multiplier — stripping it would have returned 5.0

beats.honesty_note: DELIBERATE CORRECTION, VERIFIED BY EXECUTION. The script says the regex layer turns $5.0M into 5000000.0. A regex that merely STRIPS non-numeric characters returns 5.0 — the magnitude is destroyed. The parser shown maps K/M/B to multipliers, which is what actually produces the script's stated output. Run against the script's figure it returns exactly 5000000.0. See SOURCES.md.

beats.narration_text: So stop trying to fix formatting with system prompts. Write a downstream parsing function that forces the model's unstructured text into your system's exact structural reality. Never trust a language model to format data.

props.title: parse.py
props.code:
def parse(text: str) -> float | None:
    ...

# TASK: never trust an LLM to format data.

# These four must all return 5000000.0:
#   "5000000"
#   "$5,000,000.00"
#   "5.0M"
#   "five million"
#
# And "N/A" must return None, not raise.

beats.authoring_note: The four-input test table is the reel's addition. The script's task is a slogan; this turns it into something the viewer can actually run and fail.

beats.narration_text: And once it passes those, here is the prompt worth running. Hand a model your parser and ask it for twenty number spellings a real financial document would contain that your function gets wrong. Negative values in brackets. European decimal commas. Ranges. The spellings you did not think of are the ones already in your data.
